passage:
Monday. Varun dropped the catch in the colony cricket match. At dinner Swati giggled, "Butterfingers Varun!" Mummy smiled a little, and Swati felt pleased.
Wednesday. Swati saw Varun eat a biscuit before homework. She ran to the kitchen. "Mummy, Varun's eating biscuits and he hasn't finished maths!" Mummy sighed "Varun!" from the stove. Varun glared at Swati all evening.
Saturday. Swati ran in again. "Mummy, Varun..." Mummy, rubbing her forehead, said, "Swati, not now. I'm so tired of this." Swati's smile vanished. That night Varun hid her favourite pencil box and wouldn't say where. "You always get me in trouble," he said. Nobody had won anything.

qa.q: What did Varun drop in the colony cricket match?
qa.a: Varun dropped the catch.

qa.q: How did Swati feel when Mummy smiled at 'Butterfingers Varun'?
qa.a: Swati felt pleased and proud, as if teasing Varun had won Mummy's favour.

qa.q: What could Swati try instead of running to Mummy?
qa.a: She could leave small things like the biscuit alone and fetch an adult only for real safety problems, which would keep the peace with Varun.

qa.q: How does Varun see Swati's tattling by Saturday?
qa.a: Varun feels he is always being got into trouble, so he holds a real grievance and hits back by hiding her pencil box.

grounding: Shows a child teasing and telling on a sibling to win a parent's favour, leaving a tired parent and a sibling with a real grievance.

subtype: Stage 4: The middle child's or younger one's view [Receiver]
passage:
"Can I play?" Leela stood at the terrace door with her own skipping rope.
"No, Leela, it's a big-kids' game," Lavanya said. "You'll just mess it up."
"I won't! I know the rules!"
Nakul laughed. "You can be the umpire. Sit there and don't talk."
"That's not playing. That's sitting!"
"Then go play with your dolls," said Lavanya.
Leela stamped downstairs. "Amma, they never let me play! It's not fair!"
Amma looked up from the vegetables. "What did they say?"
"That I'm a baby. I'm seven! I can count faster than Nakul!"
"You want them to take you seriously."
Leela nodded hard, her eyes full. "I want them to say 'come on, Leela' like they say to each other."
Amma put down the knife. "Let's go up together and ask which job in the game you'd really like."

qa.q: What did Nakul say Leela could be?
qa.a: He said Leela could be the umpire and should sit there and not talk.

qa.q: What does Leela want most when she complains to Amma?
qa.a: Leela feels left out and belittled, and wants the older ones to take her seriously and include her like one of them.

qa.q: How is Amma helping at this point?
qa.a: Amma listens, names that Leela wants to be taken seriously, and offers to go up together to find a real role in the game.

qa.q: How might Lavanya see having Leela in the game?
qa.a: Lavanya seems to see Leela as too little and worries the game will get messed up, without noticing how hurt Leela feels.

grounding: Shows a younger sibling bossed and left out of the older ones' games, protesting unfairness because she wants to be taken seriously.

passage: Abbu used to say, "Why can't you be neat like Rehan?" and Rehan got, "Why can't you read like Ayesha?" So we were always racing. This year something changed. After a parent-teacher meeting, Abbu stopped comparing. When I finished a whole chapter book, he said, "Ayesha, you stuck with that even when it got boring." When Rehan built the model bridge, he said, "You tried three designs. That's patience." Just about us, one at a time. And when we fought over the TV remote, he didn't come running. He said, "Sort it out, you two. Call me if someone's getting hurt." We made a timetable. My friend Sonali couldn't believe we have a remote timetable. Now I don't need to beat Rehan. I only need to beat my last book.

qa.q: What did Abbu say when Rehan built the model bridge?
qa.a: He said, "You tried three designs. That's patience."

qa.q: Why does Ayesha no longer feel a need to beat Rehan?
qa.a: Ayesha feels secure and valued for effort, so competing with Rehan no longer seems necessary.

qa.q: Which of Abbu's changes seems to have helped most?
qa.a: Praising each child's own effort without comparing, and letting them sort out small quarrels like the remote unless someone is getting hurt.

qa.q: How might Rehan feel now that he isn't compared with Ayesha?
qa.a: Rehan likely feels relieved and proud of his own patience, no longer measured against Ayesha's reading.

grounding: Shows a parent who stops comparing, praises each child's own effort and lets the children solve small quarrels, so the rivalry fades.

passage: Note for Ankita and Uday's parents, from Nana, Sunday. You asked me to write down how the week went while you were away, so here is one moment I don't want you to miss. Those two fought over the swing, the last paratha and the window seat nearly every day. But on Friday at the park, a bigger boy grabbed Uday's cricket bat and called him "shorty". Before I could even stand up, Ankita marched over and said, "Give it back. He's my brother." Uday stood right behind her, fists clenched. The boy handed the bat back. On the walk home they argued about who had been braver. I bought them both a kulfi and told them I was proud of how they stood together, not of any fighting. I think this is what you've been hoping to see.

qa.q: What did the bigger boy call Uday?
qa.a: He called him "shorty".

qa.q: How does Nana seem to feel about what happened at the park?
qa.a: Nana seems proud and moved, eager that the parents should not miss seeing the two stand together.

qa.q: What did Nana do on the walk home that encouraged the right lesson?
qa.a: Nana praised them for standing together rather than for any fighting, and treated them both to kulfi.

qa.q: What might Uday have felt when Ankita said, 'He's my brother'?
qa.a: Uday probably felt protected and proud, backing her up with clenched fists instead of feeling small.

grounding: Shows a grandparent noticing siblings who fight almost daily defending each other against an outsider, rivalry and loyalty living side by side.

passage: In a London park, two-year-old Tariq was pouring sand into a bucket beside his friend Yuki. "Time to go home now," Mama said, holding out her hand. Tariq looked at the bucket, then at Yuki, still digging. His face crumpled. His arms went stiff at his sides. "No!" he wailed, and big tears rolled down as Mama bent to pick him up.

qa.q: What was Tariq doing beside Yuki?
qa.a: He was pouring sand into a bucket.

qa.q: Why did Tariq's face crumple when Mama said it was time to go?
qa.a: He felt upset and frustrated, wanting to stay and play with Yuki but not yet able to manage that wish.

qa.q: What could Mama try next time before leaving the park?
qa.a: She could give a small warning, like 'two more buckets, then home', and name his feeling: 'You want to stay with Yuki.'

qa.q: What might Yuki experience when Tariq is carried away crying?
qa.a: Yuki may feel puzzled or a little sad to lose a digging friend so suddenly.

grounding: Shows a toddler told it is time to leave the park, unable to manage the wish to stay, crumpling into tears with a stiff body.

passage: In a busy Madrid supermarket, Mateo, almost three, dropped flat onto the cold floor by the fruit. He screamed, kicked his shoes off and arched his back like a bridge. His dad, Sami, crouched down. "Mateo, listen, we'll..." Mateo threw a mandarin, then another. He couldn't hear a word. His cheeks were scarlet and his breath came in gulps. Sami moved the bag of apples out of reach and waited.

qa.q: What did Mateo throw?
qa.a: He threw a mandarin, then another.

qa.q: What does Mateo's arching and screaming suggest about what he is feeling?
qa.a: He is overwhelmed by a huge, angry storm of feeling, far too upset to hear or reason.

qa.q: What is the most useful thing Sami can do during the peak?
qa.a: Stay close and calm, keep Mateo safe by moving things out of reach, and wait instead of trying to reason.

qa.q: What might Sami be feeling in the middle of the busy supermarket?
qa.a: Sami may feel embarrassed and stressed with people around, yet he chooses to stay calm and wait.

grounding: Shows a toddler at the peak of a tantrum, screaming, kicking, throwing and arching, unable to listen or reason.

subtype: Stage 3: Caregiver's stress and choice point [Observer]
passage: At the crowded temple fair in Pandharpur, two-year-old Shalini sat down in the dust and howled for a balloon. Tanuja felt every eye on her. An old man tutted. A woman said, "Just give her one." Tanuja's cheeks burned. She was tired from the long bus ride and wanted to shout, "Stop it!" She took one breath. Then she knelt beside Shalini, away from the stalls, and stayed there, calm and close.

qa.q: What did Shalini howl for?
qa.a: She howled for a balloon.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling as the old man tutted?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and tired, her cheeks burning, and was tempted to shout.

qa.q: Which choice did Tanuja make, and why was it the hardest but most useful?
qa.a: She took a breath and knelt calmly beside Shalini instead of shouting or giving in, keeping Shalini safe without teaching that howling works.

qa.q: What is it like for Shalini in the dust at the fair?
qa.a: Shalini is overwhelmed and upset about the balloon, too young to calm down on her own.

grounding: Shows a caregiver feeling embarrassed and tired under strangers' stares and choosing to stay calm nearby rather than shout or give in.

passage:
Monday. Eshaan, two, threw himself down when the TV went off. Tarun knelt. "You're upset. I'm here." He moved the glass cup away and waited.
Wednesday. Another storm, over shoes. Tarun knelt again, quiet and close. Eshaan kicked, then slowed sooner.
Saturday. Bath time ended. Eshaan wailed, then crawled straight into Tarun's lap, still sobbing, and let himself be held.

qa.q: What did Tarun move away on Monday?
qa.a: He moved the glass cup away.

qa.q: Why did Eshaan crawl into Tarun's lap on Saturday?
qa.a: He still felt upset, but he had come to feel safe with Tarun close by, so he looked for comfort sooner.

qa.q: What in Tarun's approach seems to help each time?
qa.a: Kneeling close, saying calmly 'You're upset. I'm here', moving dangerous things away and waiting without arguing.

qa.q: What might Tarun feel as the storms get shorter?
qa.a: Tarun may feel relieved and encouraged that staying calm and close is helping.

grounding: Shows a caregiver kneeling close, speaking softly, moving harmful objects and waiting, and a toddler learning that big feelings can be survived.

passage: Note for Sudha, from the daycare room, Tuesday. Sumit had a big cry at pick-up time today when the blocks were packed away. After a few minutes the screaming turned into hiccupping sobs. Then he held out both arms to me. I picked him up, no lecture, and just held him. I gave him a sip of water and breathed slowly with him until his chest settled. He rested his head on my shoulder. He was calm and smiling by the time you came.

qa.q: What set off Sumit's big cry?
qa.a: The blocks were packed away at pick-up time.

qa.q: What did Sumit's outstretched arms suggest he needed?
qa.a: He was winding down and needed comfort, feeling tired and sad but ready to be held.

qa.q: Why did the note-writer skip the lecture?
qa.a: At this stage Sumit needed comfort rather than words: a hug, a sip of water and slow breathing helped his body settle.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel reading this note?
qa.a: Sudha would probably feel reassured and grateful that Sumit was comforted and calm by pick-up.

grounding: Shows a toddler's crying easing into sobs as he reaches out, and a caregiver offering a hug, water and slow breaths instead of a lecture.

subtype: Stage 6: Repair and naming the feeling [Response]
passage:
At bedtime Pallavi stroked Vinita's hair.
"Park," Vinita said sleepily.
"You wanted to stay at the park. That was hard."
"Hard," Vinita said. "Cry."
"Yes, you cried. You were sad."
"Sad." Vinita touched her own cheek.
"We had to leave. And I still love you. We can go again tomorrow."
"Tomorrow swing?"
"Tomorrow swing."
Vinita smiled and closed her eyes.

qa.q: What did Vinita ask for tomorrow?
qa.a: She asked for the swing tomorrow.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel when she touched her own cheek and said 'Sad'?
qa.a: She seemed calm and comforted, starting to link the word sad with how she felt at the park.

qa.q: Which parts of Pallavi's bedtime talk help Vinita most?
qa.a: She names the feeling in simple words, keeps the limit, says she still loves Vinita, and promises they can go again tomorrow.

qa.q: What would change if Pallavi had said 'You were naughty at the park'?
qa.a: Vinita would learn shame instead of a word for her feeling, and the bond might feel less safe.

grounding: Shows a caregiver later naming a toddler's feeling in simple words, keeping the limit and making the love clear.
